title: Put Object Pronouns in the Right Place
goal: Choose and place Norwegian object pronouns correctly in simple sentences.

objectives.statement: Choose and place Norwegian object pronouns correctly in simple sentences.

sections.title: A missing key before the meeting

spans.value: Maja and Jonas are preparing a meeting room. Sara has gone out to buy coffee, and the key seems to be missing.
Har du nøkkelen til møterommet?

blocks.translation: Do you have the key to the meeting room?

spans.value: Ja, jeg har den.
Bra. Jeg finner Sara ikke—eller, vent: Jeg finner henne ikke.

blocks.translation: Good. I can’t find Sara—or, wait: I can’t find her.

spans.value: Hun kjøper kaffe. Jeg ringte henne nettopp.

blocks.translation: She is buying coffee. I just called her.

spans.value: Svarte hun?
Nei, hun svarer meg ikke.
Kan du åpne møterommet nå?

blocks.translation: Can you open the meeting room now?

spans.value: Ja, jeg kan åpne det.
The small words den, henne, meg and det prevent Maja and Jonas from repeating names and nouns. They are object pronouns (objektspronomen): pronouns used for the person or thing affected by an action.
The dialogue also shows that choosing the correct pronoun is only part of the job. Its position matters. Compare Maja’s self-correction:
A full noun such as Sara normally follows ikke in this kind of neutral sentence. A short, unstressed object pronoun such as henne normally moves in front of ikke when there is only one verb.
An object pronoun replaces a person, animal or thing already understood from the context.
The second sentence uses henne because Sara is the object of ringer: she receives the call.
The common object forms are:

items.value: den for it when replacing a masculine or feminine noun
det for it when replacing a neuter noun

spans.value: In Bokmål, han is also accepted as an object form in many contexts. This chapter uses ham because its form clearly distinguishes it from subject han.
Compare who performs the action and who receives it:
In the first sentence, hun performs the action and meg receives it. In the second, jeg performs the action and henne receives it.
For things, the grammatical gender and number of the known noun guide the choice:

no.value: Har du nøkkelen? – Ja, jeg har den.

en.value: Do you have the key? – Yes, I have it.

spans.value: Nøkkelen is masculine, so den replaces it.

no.value: Har du kortet? – Ja, jeg har det.

en.value: Do you have the card? – Yes, I have it.

spans.value: Kortet is neuter, so det replaces it.

no.value: Har du koppene? – Ja, jeg har dem.

en.value: Do you have the cups? – Yes, I have them.

spans.value: Koppene is plural, so dem replaces it.
In a simple affirmative main clause with one verb, the object pronoun normally comes after the verb.
A compact pattern is:
subject + verb + object pronoun

The pronoun stays connected to the verb even when another element begins the sentence. Norwegian main-clause word order places the verb early, but the object pronoun still follows the subject when the subject comes after that verb.

en.value: After the meeting Jonas will help us.

spans.value: Do not place the pronoun before the verb by copying English questions or other familiar patterns.
This is not normal Norwegian word order. Use:

sections.title: Object pronouns with ikke and one verb

spans.value: The important contrast appears when a simple sentence contains ikke.
With a full noun object, Norwegian commonly places ikke before the object:
With a short, unstressed object pronoun and only one verb, the pronoun normally comes before ikke:
Compare the pairs directly:

en.value: We aren’t using the meeting room.

spans.value: The compact rule for a neutral sentence with one verb is:
full noun: verb + ikke + noun
object pronoun: verb + pronoun + ikke
This movement is sometimes called object shift, but the practical choice matters more than the label: if a short object pronoun replaces a known noun, put it before ikke in this one-verb pattern.
A common mistake is to assume that ikke always comes immediately after the verb.
This order can occur when meg is strongly contrasted or emphasized, as in not me, but someone else. For an ordinary neutral statement, use:
At this level, use the neutral pattern unless the context clearly demands strong contrast.

sections.title: When the sentence has two verbs

spans.value: Do not move every object pronoun in front of ikke. When a sentence has a modal verb plus an infinitive, the object belongs with the infinitive.
Here, kan is followed by the main action åpne. The object det follows åpne.

en.value: Maja is going to call her.
Maja is not going to call her.

spans.value: The same principle applies when har is used with a past participle:
Compare one verb and two verbs:
In the first sentence, finner is the only verb, so henne comes before ikke. In the second, henne is the object of finne and stays after that infinitive.
Another aligned contrast:

en.value: She isn’t going to call me.

spans.value: The meaning is similar, but the verb structure changes the pronoun’s position.
The compact distinction is:
one verb: verb + pronoun + ikke
two verbs: first verb + ikke + second verb + pronoun
A frequent error is to apply the one-verb rule mechanically:
Use:
Sara returns with the coffee. Maja now has to work out what happened to the key and access card.
Hei! Ringte dere meg?
Ja, Jonas ringte deg, men du svarte ham ikke.

blocks.translation: Yes, Jonas called you, but you didn’t answer him.

spans.value: Beklager. Jeg hørte telefonen ikke—nei, jeg hørte den ikke.

blocks.translation: Sorry. I didn’t hear the phone—no, I didn’t hear it.

spans.value: Det går bra. Nå kan vi åpne møterommet.

blocks.translation: That’s fine. Now we can open the meeting room.

spans.value: Har dere adgangskortet?

blocks.translation: Do you have the access card?

spans.value: Nei, vi har ikke funnet det.
Vent! Du ga meg det tidligere, Maja. Det ligger i lomma mi.

blocks.translation: Wait! You gave it to me earlier, Maja. It’s in my pocket.

spans.value: The returning scene reuses all three decisions:

items.value: deg, ham, den and det refer to known people or things.
A one-verb negative sentence places the pronoun before ikke: du svarte ham ikke and jeg hørte den ikke.
A two-verb negative sentence keeps the pronoun after the main action: vi har ikke funnet det.

sections.title: Cumulative transfer: preparing for a birthday visit

spans.value: Move to a new everyday situation. Nora and Emil are preparing to visit a friend. They need to find a present, contact their friend and bring some cakes.

Without looking back, explain the placement difference among these three sentence types: an affirmative sentence, a negative sentence with one verb, and a negative sentence with two verbs. Then produce one Norwegian example of each using the same object pronoun. A successful review shows that you can retrieve the placement pattern and transfer it to a new everyday context.

prompt.value: Choose the one complete object-pronoun set that fits all five meeting-room exchanges.

options.text: 1. Jeg ringer ham. 2. Maja hjelper henne. 3. Ja, jeg har den. 4. Ja, jeg har det. 5. Ja, jeg har dem.
options.why: ham and henne do not match the genders of Sara and Jonas in these lines.

options.text: 1. Jeg ringer henne. 2. Maja hjelper ham. 3. Ja, jeg har den. 4. Ja, jeg har det. 5. Ja, jeg har dem.
options.why: Sara is feminine, Jonas is masculine, nøkkelen is masculine, kortet is neuter, and koppene is plural; the pronouns match each reference.

options.text: 1. Jeg ringer henne. 2. Maja hjelper ham. 3. Ja, jeg har det. 4. Ja, jeg har den. 5. Ja, jeg har dem.
options.why: den and det are reversed for nøkkelen and kortet.

options.text: 1. Jeg ringer henne. 2. Maja hjelper ham. 3. Ja, jeg har den. 4. Ja, jeg har det. 5. Ja, jeg har den.
options.why: koppene is plural, so dem is required instead of den.

explanation.value: An unstressed object pronoun normally precedes ikke, while a full noun object normally follows it.
